subject: Editor’s Choice: Britain’s cost of working crisis
body: Plus, Venezuela’s oil money, Zelenskyy’s crisis and how to get into Berghain ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Roula Khalaf Editor ‌ ‌ July 25 2026 Hello from London where we have our fifth prime minister in four years. After a long build-up, Andy Burnham officially took over from Keir Starmer on Monday, pledging yet another fresh start. He purged many Starmerites from the cabinet and sprang a surprise with the appointment of John Healey, the former defence secretary who had resigned under Starmer, as his chancellor. Our expectation had been that the job would go to Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary. She is now staying in her current role. In a series of announcements, Burnham pledged to ease the cost of living by removing VAT on energy bills, capping single bus fares at £2, and slashing business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues. Small, popular measures should buy him some time. But as our consumer editor Claer Barrett argues in her hugely popular column, Burnham must also turn his attention to a looming “cost of working crisis”. The new PM may have been cheered by lower than expected inflation and higher than expected business and consumer confidence data this week, but the relief may be shortlived. Oil prices hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May on Thursday after US President Donald Trump said he was considering “a massive attack” on Iran. We will be closely monitoring the situation over the weekend and will keep you up to date on ft.com. Andy Burnham outside 10 Downing Street on Monday © Dan Kitwood/Getty Images MY CHOICES THIS WEEK ‌ ‌ 1. We scooped the Trump administration’s announcement of a fresh round of duties on global trading partners. Here’s a rundown of the winners and losers of Trump’s new tariff regime. 2. Washington has collected more than $13bn in revenues from Venezuelan oil sales this year, according to FT analysis. But it’s not clear where exactly the earthquake-shattered country’s funds are going. 3. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy replaced the commander-in-chief of Ukraine’s armed forces in the biggest shake-up to the country’s military leadership since 2024. Our Kyiv correspondent has all the details you need to know. 4. OpenAI said its agent escaped company controls and carried out a major hack. Find out why staff involved in testing and training at the San Francisco lab were unsurprised but completely “freaked out” by the incident. 5. The US signed an agreement to help Saudi Arabia develop a civilian nuclear programme, which Trump later insisted was conditional on Riyadh normalising relations with Israel. As our editorial board argues, the deal could carry serious proliferation risks. 6. A proposal by Trump’s social media company to charge for high-speed access to the president’s posts has not gone down well on Wall Street. People familiar with the matter told the FT that access was being touted at a fee of $100,000 a month. 7. Our reporters discovered that a betting account registered to George Cottrell’s name received almost $9mn in cryptocurrency from unidentified sources while he was providing gifts and benefits to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. 8. The head of an ethical fintech backed by Standard Chartered previously sought to set up arms deals with Jan Marsalek, the Wirecard executive who fled to Russia following the German company’s collapse. Read more on the latest twist in the Marsalek story. 9. Berghain has become one of the defining symbols of Berlin’s post Wall-hedonistic identity. But passing its door policy is no easy feat. Our Berlin bureau chief tells you how she got in to the notoriously selective club — on her third try. 10. You will undoubtedly have heard of “forever” chemicals — the kind that accumulate in our bodies over the years and are passed from mother to child. But should we care about them? Here’s what FT climate reporter Kenza Bryan learnt on her quest to detoxify her life. On the latest episode of our video podcast The Story of Money, host Robin Wigglesworth and the FT’s US financial commentator Robert Armstrong explore the extraordinary life of the greatest day trader in history. body: Plus: Welcome to the era of candyfloss finance ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser THE ROCK STAR AI FOUNDER Alice Fishburn Opinion and Analysis Editor ‌ ‌ July 25 2026 Another month, another record-breaking AI model release. This time it came in the guise of Kimi K3 from the Chinese company Moonshot. At its helm is founder Yang Zhilin. Eleanor Olcott and Zijing Wu have produced a great profile of the man who wanted to be a rock star but had to settle for groundbreaking technological breakthroughs instead. Andy Burnham became prime minister on Monday (after what felt like a VERY long run-up). This week has seen a dribbling out of measures and various trips around the country. Philip Stephens writes for us about why instead of looking to 21st-century Manchester as his model for devolution, Burnham should consider 19th-century Birmingham. The Victorians had a lot to teach us. I really enjoyed this piece by the one and only Gillian Tett on why we are once again living in an era of financial candyfloss. The sugar cloud is being spun finer and finer and it may well end in a sticky mess. Finally, a wonerful obit to see out the week (and probably the last bit of football commentary in a rich summer of it). The late, great Kevin Keegan. Have a good weekend.
